content:
Bloomberg reports that bipartisan US senators are pressing Apple CEO Tim Cook to commit by August 21 not to use memory chips from Chinese suppliers CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Here are the details.

A little background

Apple is trying to navigate an ongoing memory shortage and has reportedly sought approval from the Trump administration to source components from CXMT and Yangtze Memory. Both companies have been designated as Chinese military companies by the US Department of Defense.

Legally, Apple does not need US government approval to purchase chips from these two companies, but moving forward without government backing could expose the company to significant political consequences.

As a result, Tim Cook told The Wall Street Journal in an interview ahead of Apple's recent price increases that "all options should be on the table," adding that "we should be looking at all sources of supply."

The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Apple had sought a waiver from the government to purchase chips from CXMT. Separately, the Financial Times reported that Apple was in talks to procure chips from Yangtze Memory. The FT later further disclosed that Apple is already testing CXMT's DRAM chips.

The Wall Street Journal had earlier reported that Apple's use of Chinese memory chips might extend beyond the China market, with the company seeking government approval to use CXMT and Yangtze Memory components in products sold outside the US as well.

That report also detailed Micron's efforts to lobby the government to reject Apple's requests, arguing that letting Chinese suppliers into Apple's supply chain could harm the domestic memory industry.

This is not Apple's first attempt to source memory chips from Yangtze Memory. In 2022, the company explored using the supplier's components in some China-sold iPhones, but shelved the plan after it drew the attention of US lawmakers and ran into tighter export controls.

At the time, then-Senate Intelligence Committee vice chairman Marco Rubio accused Apple of "playing with fire," and lawmakers from both parties warned that the deal could pose a national security risk.

Lawmakers pile on again

Bloomberg reports today that "a bipartisan group of US senators is pressing Apple to abandon any move to source chips from blacklisted Chinese semiconductor suppliers [CXMT] and [Yangtze Memory], warning that the iPhone maker could become reliant on an American rival for a critical component."

According to the report, the lawmakers criticized Apple's plan as "short-sighted," saying it would "further entangle the world's most valuable consumer electronics company in a critical component supplied by a company the US government has formally designated as a Chinese military company."

The lawmakers also pointed out that other companies could follow Apple's lead, which would in turn hurt the domestic memory industry as well as planned investments in states such as Indiana, Idaho, New York and Virginia.

They added that any initial restriction limiting CXMT memory to China-sold products is unlikely to hold for long, because "once a component is qualified through Apple's manufacturing, extending it globally is only a procurement decision away."

Finally, beyond demanding that Apple commit by August 21 to "avoid using CXMT or Yangtze Memory memory in its products," the senators also asked Apple to disclose any information it shared with CXMT during the component qualification process, noting that transferring controlled technical data to advanced Chinese chipmaking facilities may require Commerce Department authorization.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's inquiry.
